title: Using Artificial Intelligence Algorithms to Predict Self-Reported Problem Gambling Among Online Casino Gamblers from Different Countries Using Account-Based Player Data
authors: Hopfgartner, N.; Auer, M.; Helic, D.; Griffiths, M.
venue: International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction
tldr: Behavioral variables like frequent in-session depositing and account depletion predict self-reported problem gambling more effectively than monetary intensity variables across British, Canadian, and Spanish online casino gamblers.
problem_and_motivation: Online gambling operators need early detection models for problem gambling, but existing research predominantly uses voluntary self-exclusion as a proxy measure, which is unreliable. The few studies combining self-reported problem gambling with objective player-tracking data are limited to single countries, leaving cross-country generalizability untested. Understanding whether behavioral patterns predict problem gambling independently of monetary expenditure across different regulatory contexts is essential for developing universally applicable responsible gambling tools.
approach: Analyzed a secondary dataset of 1743 British, Canadian, and Spanish online casino gamblers who completed the PGSI, with 30 days of player-tracking data preceding completion.
Applied hierarchical logistic regression with three variable categories: demographics, behavioral features, and monetary intensity variables, using backward elimination for feature selection.
Tested five machine learning models (AdaBoost, decision trees, extra-trees, gradient boosting, random forests) in cross-country leave-one-out and full-dataset train-test configurations.

Constructed two novel behavioral metrics: regular account depletion (percentage of sessions ending with low balance) and frequent depositing (average deposits per session) to capture impulsivity indicators.
findings: Behavioral variables including self-exclusions, frequent in-session depositing, and account depletion were significant predictors of self-reported problem gambling, while monetary intensity variables showed no significant improvement.
num: 27.4% of the sample scored 8+ on the PGSI indicating problem gambling, with Canadian gamblers showing the highest prevalence at 35.2%.
ML models trained on all three countries outperformed leave-one-out models, with random forest achieving the highest ROC-AUC of 0.717 for Canada.
Models trained without a specific country's data still weakly generalized, suggesting universal behavioral patterns across cultural and regulatory boundaries.
num: The baseline model using only total deposits had ROC-AUC of approximately 0.5, performing no better than random chance.
key_figures_tables: Figure 1: PGSI score distribution before and after data cleaning → removing rapid responders eliminated extreme score spikes at 0 and 27.
Figure 3: Hierarchical regression coefficients → behavioral variables (self-exclusions, session length, depositing frequency, account depletion) were significant predictors across countries.
Table 1: Descriptive statistics by country → Canadian gamblers had highest mean PGSI (7.11) and problem gambling prevalence (35.2%).
Table 4: Model fit statistics → adding behavioral features significantly improved Nagelkerke R2 and reduced AIC compared to control models.
Table 5: ML model ROC-AUC values → including country-specific data generally enhanced predictive performance across all models.

topics.name: Anomaly Detection Algorithms for Personal Spending Data
topics.justification: Directly applies ML algorithms to detect anomalous behavioral patterns (frequent depositing, account depletion) predictive of problem gambling from account-based tracking data.

topics.name: Classification Approaches for Financial Behavioral Profiles
topics.justification: Demonstrates classification of behavioral profiles into problem and non-problem categories using hierarchical regression and ensemble ML methods.

topics.name: Evaluation of Algorithmic Modules
topics.justificance: Evaluates five ML models using ROC-AUC with cross-country validation, comparing behavioral versus monetary feature sets.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper demonstrates that behavioral variables are superior to monetary intensity variables for predicting self-reported problem gambling across different countries. It introduces two novel behavioral metrics (regular account depletion and frequent depositing) that capture impulsivity indicators. The cross-country analysis reveals that while country-specific data improves model performance, universal behavioral patterns exist that generalize across cultural and regulatory boundaries. The hierarchical modeling approach provides a methodological framework for separating demographic, behavioral, and monetary contributions to problem gambling prediction.
directly_justifies: Behavioral variables including self-exclusions, frequent in-session depositing, and account depletion are significant predictors of self-reported problem gambling.
Monetary intensity variables do not significantly improve prediction when behavioral features are already included.
ML models can weakly generalize across countries without country-specific training data, suggesting universal behavioral patterns.
The baseline model using only total deposits performs no better than random chance (ROC-AUC approximately 0.5).
limits: Self-selection bias due to voluntary PGSI completion inflates problem gambling prevalence rates compared to national estimates.
Self-reported data may be compromised by memory recall, social desirability bias, and subjective self-assessment.
Relatively small sample size after data cleaning (1743 from 6352) may limit statistical power.
30-day observation period may not capture long-term behavioral trends captured by the PGSI's 12-month scope.

Topic 5.C (Classification Approaches for Financial Behavioral Profiles) was flagged as medium relevance because the paper classifies users into behavioral profiles (problem vs. non-problem gamblers) using regression and ensemble methods. Topic 12.B (Evaluation of Algorithmic Modules) was flagged as medium relevance for the systematic comparison of five ML models with cross-country validation. Topics 1-3 (Filipino demographics, cultural practices, expense categorization) were rejected as the paper focuses on gambling behavior in European and Canadian contexts. Topics 4.A-4.B (landscape of personal finance systems) were rejected as the paper addresses gambling platforms, not personal finance management. Topics 6-7 (predictive modeling, budgeting) were considered but the paper focuses on classification rather than forecasting or budget allocation. Topics 9-14 were rejected as the paper does not cover mobile design, privacy, engagement, savings, debt, synthetic data, or ML deployment. The paper is most aligned with anomaly detection and behavioral classification domains.
